description: Hey, we are a bunch of students from UofR!!
summary:
We got to the moon, have sent probes out into the universe, and have reliable satellites that can be controlled from the ground. Now soon, we explore Mars for the first time with our own eyes rather than a satellite or photos taken through a rover. 

The Astronauts on Mars will need a map to help them with navigating their newfound terrain. They will need to know where the safe slopes are, how long it takes to get from one place to another, how much climbing is involved, and what it looks like when you get there.

Mars Map is that map.

It is a web app that combines a 3D globe of Mars, 2-metre terrain built from NASA HiRISE stereo data, a slope-hazard layer, mineral and science layers
details:
What it does

Mars Map is a layered, hyperlocal map for planning and rehearsing a Marswalk. In orbit view, an astronaut searches a landmark, flies to a site and switches on data layers: a green/yellow/red slope-hazard map, mineral and science layers for choosing targets, and rover stops. Clicking two points returns a route over the real terrain that goes around steep ground rather than over it, with distance, ascent, estimated time, steepest slope and an elevation profile. Three travel modes (on foot, robotic rover, pressurized crewed rover) each have their own speed and slope limit, and both can be edited. Ground view lets the astronaut walk the site at eye height on a 2 m terrain mesh. Mars view is a street-view-style viewer built from real Navcam frames, placed on the horizon by compass direction so the crew sees exactly what they will see on arrival.

How it works

We crop NASA/USGS 1 m HiRISE digital terrain models of Jezero (Mars 2020 TRN mosaic) and Gale (MSL merged DEM) into 6 × 6 km, 2 m grids, reprojected so every cell is a true metre on the ground. Slope is computed with Horn's method, the same used by GDAL and ArcGIS. Travel cost follows Tobler's hiking function, with ground steeper than 25° impassable on foot, and routes are found by least-cost search over the full grid. Rover stops and images come from NASA's Mars 2020 and MSL waypoint maps and raw-image feed; each frame's direction is computed from the camera axis rotated by the rover's attitude. The global planet comes from the Cesium Mars 3D Tiles; near a site, it is replaced by our 36×-finer local terrain.

Why it matters

The challenge asks for a map a crew could use for one excursion, with at least three kinds of data layered together and astronaut safety first. Mars Map layers topography, derived slope hazards, mineral and science data, orbital imagery and rover surface photos into a single view, and it turns them into decisions: which path, how long, how much oxygen-time, and whether the interesting rock is safe to reach. The same tool serves crews, mission planners comparing foot and rover traverses, and scientists linking a target to the images taken there.

How we checked our work

We tested our coordinate convention against Cesium's Mars terrain at 275 points (correlation 1.000 using planetocentric latitude, 0.615 otherwise) and measured the 74 m vertical offset between the two datasets rather than assuming it. The routing engine has 33 automated tests covering hazard avoidance, detours, slope limits and real Jezero routes. We state our assumptions openly: Tobler's curve comes from Earth hikers and the crewed-rover speed is an estimate, and both are single parameters that can be refitted to suited-mobility data.

What's next

Jezero and Gale were chosen because rover ground truth lets us validate the map; the pipeline takes one DEM and a few commands to add any candidate human landing site. Radiation and atmospheric layers, HiRISE orthophoto textures and consumables-aware routing are the next steps.

Humanity has already reached the stars. Let us make the map.
